newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALGERIA ASKED TO PROBE REPORTED DEATH IN CUSTODY.
newsitem.headline: ALGERIA ASKED TO PROBE REPORTED DEATH IN CUSTODY.

text.p: A U.S.-based human rights group has asked Algeria to investigate whether an alleged mastermind behind the assassination of Algeria's top trade union leader was executed without trial while in custody.

In a faxed statement late on Wednesday, Human Rights Watch said Rachid Medjahed, who had been shown on television confessing to directing the killing of Abdelhak Benhamouda, had died while in detention.

"The information that we collected during our recent visit (to Algeria) gives rise to concern that Mr Medjahed was extrajudicially executed while in custody," Human Rights Watch said in a letter to Algeria's Justice Minister Mohamed Adami.
It added: "It is clear, moreover, that authorities have actively sought to cover up, rather than expose what happened to Mr Medjahed between his arrest and death."

Human Rights Watch said Medjahed, aged about 30, "appeared to be in physical and psychological distress" during his televised "confession". It said his 25-year-old wife Samira Mizreb was still in detention in late April.

Benhamouda, head of Algeria's million-strong UGTA union, was gunned down in central Algiers last January. He had earlier announced he was quitting the UGTA to form a political party to contest next June's parliamentary elections.
The authorities said Moslem fundamentalists killed him.
Human Rights Watch said Medjahed's death thwarted a trial and "further clouds efforts to identify the labour leader's assassins".

It accepted that Benhamouda was strongly anti-Islamist but added that "many observers have speculated that he had also earned the enmity of factions within the country's leadership" over his plans to set up a party expected to support President Liamine Zeroual.

Algeria's president sees the June election as a way to bring the country out of over five years of violence in which about 60,000 people have died. It erupted when the authorities in 1992 cancelled a general election in which the Islamic Salvation Front, now banned, had taken a huge lead.
